claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the compared equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after similar thermomechanical processing.
The quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater resistance to dislocation motion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater resistance to dislocation motion gives the quinary alloy higher strength during deformation than the lower-component subsets.
Greater resistance to dislocation motion alters failure modes in the quinary alloy relative to the lower-component subsets.
The full complement of elements in the quinary alloy produces greater local lattice distortion than occurs in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The full complement of elements in the quinary alloy produces greater variation in the local electronic environment than occurs in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Local lattice distortion and atomic-level compositional fluctuations influence dislocation-core structures.
Local lattice distortion and atomic-level compositional fluctuations influence slip-system activation.
Lattice distortions and local electronic-environment variations make dislocation cores more irregular.
The proposed lattice and electronic variations impede dislocation glide.
The proposed lattice and electronic variations increase the thermal activation-energy barrier for slip.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower activation energies for slip.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower strain-rate sensitivity.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strengths.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit less irregular dislocation cores than the quinary alloy.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will require a lower stress level to produce strain-rate changes than the quinary alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies when the compared alloys remain single-phase FCC and thermally activated dislocation motion dominates.
